---
title: "Brain region mappings"
---

A mapping is a choice of how finely to describe anatomy. The Allen hierarchy has thousands of
regions; almost no analysis wants that many. A mapping picks a level of the
[structure tree](brain-region-hierarchy.qmd) and collapses everything below it.

## The four mappings

| Mapping | Regions | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Allen** | 1328 | You want the full Allen parcellation; the default |
| **Beryl** | 308 | A middle granularity, the usual choice for brain-wide summaries (IBL) |
| **Cosmos** | 12 | Coarse, major divisions only (IBL) |
| **Swanson** | 323 | You are plotting on the Swanson flat map |

![The Allen, Beryl and Cosmos mappings on one coronal slice (AP −1.6 mm), and the Swanson mapping as the flat map, since Swanson regions have no 3D position. Every voxel takes the Allen colour of its mapped target, so coarser mappings give fewer, larger patches. The counts are regions present on this slice, not the totals in the table.](images/mappings-coronal.png)

## Beryl and Cosmos

Beryl and Cosmos are coarser mappings developed by the IBL in consultation with the Steinmetz
lab. Each is defined as a list of Allen region ids (`beryl.npy` and `cosmos.npy`, see
[Data files](data-files.qmd)); every region below one of those ids is collapsed into it.

- **Beryl** keeps 308 regions, a middle granularity between the full Allen parcellation and
  the major divisions. It is the usual choice for summarising results across the whole brain.
- **Cosmos** keeps 12, the major divisions of the brain. Use it when you want
  one value per large area, such as isocortex, thalamus or cerebellum.

To apply either one to your own region ids, see
[Remap region ids](../how-to/remap-region-ids.ipynb).

## What a mapping actually stores

A mapping stores, for each of the 2655 regions, the **index of the highest-level ancestor that
should be considered**. Every region below that node is given its parent's annotation.

```python
br.mappings['Beryl']        # 2655 indices -> 308 distinct targets
br.mappings.keys()          # the eight mappings
```

So mapping is not lookup, it is collapse: `MOp1`, `MOp2/3`, `MOp5` and `MOp6a` all resolve to
whatever ancestor the mapping terminates at. Nothing is lost from the tree itself — the
mapping is a view over it.

Each mapping has an `-lr` lateralised twin, so `br.mappings` holds eight keys in all. The plain
variant merges hemispheres; the `-lr` variant keeps them apart using the negative-id
convention. Allen has 1328 targets against Allen-lr's 2655; Swanson has 323 against
Swanson-lr's 645.

## The Swanson mapping

The Swanson mapping belongs to the Swanson flat map, a two-dimensional drawing of the brain's
regions that comes from Hahn et al. (2021); see [Citations](../citations.qmd). The mapping has
323 targets, of which the flat map draws 319. Unlike the other
mappings it has no spatial position: a region maps to a patch on the flat map, not to voxels.

To plot on the flat map, see [Plotting brain region values on the Swanson flat map](../how-to/plot-on-swanson-flatmap.ipynb).

### Which regions can be plotted

A region can be plotted if it is one of the drawn Swanson regions, or an ancestor of one. A
region outside that set has no patch to fill. Passing one does not raise an error: the
region is filled with `empty_color` (`'silver'` by default), so it appears in silver on the
figure.

### Plotting a parent region

A value passed for a parent region propagates down to all its descendants, via
`BrainRegions.propagate_down`. `Isocortex` has 374 descendants, 40 of which are Swanson
regions, so one value for `Isocortex` colours 40 separate patches identically:

```python
idx, vals = br.propagate_down(np.array(['Isocortex']), np.array([1.0]))
len(idx)   # 374 descendants
```

This paints a coarse region across a wide area. The plot shows 40 patches that share one
underlying value.

### Hemispheres

`br.mappings['Swanson']` holds a single hemisphere and contains no negative ids. Only
`Swanson-lr` carries both, with 322 negative entries.

To show the two hemispheres differently, pass signed Allen ids rather than acronyms: an
acronym such as `MOp` is identical on both sides and cannot say which one you mean.
`plot_swanson_vector` takes the absolute value of negative ids when `hemisphere` is anything
other than `'both'`, so signed ids passed with another `hemisphere` setting merge the two
sides.
